segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

In the last lab you cleaned the marks file. Today you use the clean version, `marks_clean.csv`, to answer a real question: which subject has the highest average mark, and by how much? You will compute the average per subject with `groupby()`, draw a **bar chart** with Matplotlib (bars suit a comparison between categories; a line chart would wrongly suggest the subjects are connected in order) and save it as `chart.png`, because the lab has no screen to show it on. Then you will write two or three sentences of genuine interpretation: a claim about the data such as *Science is highest, but only just*, not *the bars are blue*. Your program also writes the `README.md` every GitHub project needs, with its purpose, data source and limitations. Pushing the project to GitHub with `git init`, `git add .`, `git commit` and `git push` is your homework; this lab checks the chart, the interpretation and the README.

lab.title: Chart the averages and write the README
lab.objective: Compute the average mark per subject, save a bar chart, write a real interpretation and generate a README with purpose, data source and limitations.
lab.instructions:
The clean file marks_clean.csv (columns student, subject, marks; 40 rows) is in your working directory. Write a program that:

1. Loads it with pd.read_csv() into df.
2. Computes averages = df.groupby("subject")["marks"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) and prints one line per subject, highest first, in the form Subject: average, for example:
Science: 78.5
3. Draws a bar chart of averages with plt.bar(averages.index, averages.values), gives it a title and axis labels, and saves it with plt.savefig("chart.png"). Then prints: Chart saved to chart.png
4. Stores interpretation, a string of 2-3 sentences (at least 20 words) that makes a real claim: name the subject with the highest average, the subject just behind it and how big the gap between them is. Print it as Interpretation: <text>.
5. Writes a file README.md with these Markdown headings, each followed by one or two sentences: a title line starting with #, then ## Purpose, ## Data source (name the file marks_clean.csv) and ## Limitations (for example: only 8 students, three marks were filled with the average, the data is fictional). Then prints: README.md written
lab.constraints: Use pandas and matplotlib. Keep the names df, averages and interpretation. Save the chart to chart.png (there is no screen, so plt.show() does nothing). The README must be written by your program to README.md. No input().

plt.bar(averages.index, averages.values) draws the bars. Add plt.title(...), plt.xlabel("Subject"), plt.ylabel("Average mark") and then plt.savefig("chart.png"). For the README, build one string with the headings and write it with open("README.md", "w") as f: f.write(readme).

Read your own printed averages: the top subject is Science and Math is just behind it. Write interpretation like: "Science has the highest average at 78.5, but it is only 1.5 marks ahead of Math. History is far behind at 64.25, so that is where the class needs help."

lab.solution:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Load the cleaned data
df = pd.read_csv("marks_clean.csv")

# 2. Average mark per subject, highest first
averages = df.groupby("subject")["marks"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
for subject, avg in averages.items():
    print(f"{subject}: {avg}")

# 3. Bar chart saved to a file
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.bar(averages.index, averages.values)
plt.title("Average marks per subject")
plt.xlabel("Subject")
plt.ylabel("Average mark")
plt.savefig("chart.png")
print("Chart saved to chart.png")

# 4. Interpretation: a real claim about the data
interpretation = (
    "Science has the highest average mark at 78.5, but it is only 1.5 marks ahead of Math at 77.0, "
    "so the two subjects are almost level. History is clearly the weakest subject at 64.25, more than "
    "14 marks behind Science, and that is the real gap the class should work on."
)
print("Interpretation:", interpretation)

# 5. README written by the program
readme = """# Class marks mini-project

## Purpose
Clean a class marks file and draw a bar chart of the average mark per subject.

## Data source
marks_clean.csv: fictional marks for 8 students in 5 subjects (40 rows), the cleaned output of the Lecture 25 lab.

## Limitations
Only 8 students, so one very high or very low mark moves a subject average a lot. Three missing marks were filled with the class average. The data is invented for practice.
"""
with open("README.md", "w") as f:
    f.write(readme)
print("README.md written")
